title: The Accuracy of Prediction Equations for Estimating 1-RM Performance in the Bench Press, Squat, and Deadlift
authors: LeSuer DA, McCormick JH, Mayhew JL, Wasserstein RL, Arnold MD
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: 67 untrained college students (40 men and 27 women) enrolled in weight-training classes who did four 45-minute practice sessions before testing. Not runners.
findings: The study compared the accuracy of 7 equations that predict a 1RM from repetitions to fatigue, for the bench press, the squat and the deadlift, against the 1RM each student achieved.
All correlations between predicted and achieved 1RM were high (r above 0.95).

For the bench press, the average difference between achieved and predicted weight was significantly different from zero in all but 2 of the equations; for the squat, in all but 1; and all of the equations significantly underestimated the deadlift despite the high correlations.
limitations: Only the abstract was read, on the publisher's page (the journal's own record; the paper is not indexed by PubMed or Europe PMC); the full text is behind the publisher's access control and was not fetched. The abstract does not name the 7 equations, the number of repetitions used or the direction of the bench-press and squat differences, so it does not say which way the engine's form is biased. Untrained college students, 1997, one session; no runners.
implications: Equations that rank people correctly can still be biased in absolute terms: on the squat, 6 of 7 equations differed significantly from the achieved 1RM, and on the bench press 5 of 7. An estimate of a maximum from repetitions is a label and not a test, as the engine already labels it. The deadlift was underestimated by all of them, so the bias is not the same for every lift.
It gives no value for `f8.e1rmDivisor` and does not say whether the linear form with a divisor of 30 is among the equations that were unbiased.

r1.note: The abstract was read on the publisher's page on 2026-10-31 and every finding is its own wording. The DOI resolves in Crossref, which lists no updated-by notice. The full text was not read.

r2.note: Five named authors; the publisher page lists the affiliations: Washburn University (Health, Physical Education & Exercise Science; Academic Affairs), the Human Performance Lab of Northeast Missouri State University, the Wellness/Fitness Lab of Clark College and Popeye's Cardio Fitness Center, Topeka. r3.note: Published 1997, not corrected. nuzzo-2023-reps-at-percent-1rm (7289 people, 269 studies) supersedes it for the repetitions at a percentage of 1RM; the claim here, that the equations are biased, is consistent with it.

r4.note: Consistent with reynolds-2006-1rm-prediction (the repetition-load relation is nonlinear, so a linear equation holds only to about 10 repetitions) and nuzzo-2023-reps-at-percent-1rm. Different samples and lifts; none names the equations compared here.

r5.note: Population stated: 67 untrained college students, bench press, squat and deadlift. Use for runners, for the squat and hinge lifts of the catalogue, and for a maximum estimated from repetitions plus reported repetitions in reserve is extrapolated.

r6.note: A journal paper keeps the level of its design (a cross-sectional study, level C); the caps by class are for sources outside the journals.
